settings.standfirst: Not vanity. Vigilance. And you've never told anyone you do it.
settings.lead: Five things are happening in your face at the same time. Almost everything you've tried was built for one of them.
settings.image_alt: A woman leaning close to a corporate bathroom mirror under fluorescent light, pulling her cheek taut with two fingers, no makeup.

settings.text: The fifth one is the one you're doing yourself. Start there if you only have a minute.

settings.heading: Everyone on the call saw it before you did.

settings.alt: Seen from behind, a woman at a desk reaching up to tilt her laptop screen downward during a video call, the call grid blurred.

settings.content: You tilt the screen so they only see the top of your head. Self-view stays off — because the second you watch it happen, it happens faster.
You sit by the window all year. They think you're cold. You're managing a condition none of them know you have.

settings.text: None of that is about beauty. It's infrastructure — and it runs during every meeting you've ever had.

settings.heading: Six products failed. Every one of them worked.

settings.alt: Overhead view into an open bathroom drawer holding eleven abandoned skincare products: creased tubes, a jar crusted at the rim, clogged pumps, torn sachets. All unbranded, all used, none finished.
settings.caption: Not one of these was cheap. Not one of them was finished.

settings.content: Thousands spent. Laser, prescriptions, the expensive barrier cream. And always the same pattern: what works one week won't the next.
They weren't bad products. Each one did its job — on one lever out of five. Pull one while the other four keep running, and you get exactly what you got.

settings.text: The villain was never in the bottle. It was the assumption that this has one point of attack.

settings.content: Every year the alarm fires a little easier. The nerves get a little quicker. The vessels stay open a little longer. That's how a face that used to flush and settle becomes a face with a background level it never drops below.

settings.heading: Trying to stop it is what keeps it going.

settings.alt: Extreme macro of a cheek: unretouched skin showing diffuse redness and fine branching telangiectasia — thin red vessels just under the surface.

settings.content: You get so anxious about flushing in the meeting that it happens. They notice. You lose your sentence. It climbs.

That's not willpower failing. It's a feedback path — attention recruits the flush. Four of the five levers are physical. This one can't go in a bottle, which is why no brand has ever mentioned it to you.

settings.aria_label: A loop: it starts, you watch it, it climbs, and back to the beginning.

settings.content:
• Alarm. Fires at things it shouldn't. Doesn't switch off after.
  • Nerves. Recalibrated by the alarm. Now they fire at heat you'd never feel on your arm.
  • Vessels. Open on cue, and no longer close all the way behind them.
  • Barrier. Thin enough that everything you apply becomes a new trigger.
  • Loop. Watching for it recruits it.

settings.text: Pull all five at once and the face does the rest. That's the Reset Complex™ — our reading of it, not a trial result.

settings.content: You read a hundred times that niacinamide is gentle. Then you checked the primer you'd used for two years, and there it was.
The molecule was never the problem. The dose was. The category pushes 10% because it photographs well on a label. Here it's held at 3–5%, on purpose.

settings.question: $72 is more than I want to risk on a maybe.
settings.answer:
Right objection after six failures. It's about $9 a week against what you already spend on concealer and on the products you abandon half-used.

And the 60-day refund means the money isn't at risk — no forms, no return shipping, opened bottles count. The only real commitment is eight weeks of two minutes a day.

settings.question: Will it burn? Everything burns.
settings.answer:
We can't promise it won't, and any brand promising that about a face it's never seen is guessing. What we can tell you is what came out: zero fragrance, zero essential oils, zero alcohol, zero menthol, niacinamide held at 3–5% instead of 10%.

Azelaic acid at 10% can tingle for the first minute in week one — expected, and it settles. Patch test along the jaw for three days. Stings past the first minute? Stop and take the refund.

settings.question: How is this different from the vessel-constricting creams?
settings.answer: Opposite mechanism. Those force the vessels shut from outside — which is why they act within the hour, and why they rebound wider once the active clears. There's none of that here. This works on the four levers that keep the vessels reactive in the first place.

settings.question: Isn't azelaic acid what my dermatologist already gave me?
settings.answer: Possibly — and if prescription azelaic acid alone is working, stay on it. The difference isn't the molecule. On its own it pulls one lever. The other four are what it's paired with here, at doses chosen not to fight it.

settings.question: Can I use it with my prescription?
settings.answer: Usually, and many people do — but ask whoever prescribed it. Take them the percentages above. Apply them at different times of day rather than layering.

settings.question: I'm pregnant or breastfeeding.
settings.answer: Ask your doctor or OB first and take them the percentages. We're not going to tell you it's safe — that's not a claim we're in a position to make about a leave-on used twice daily for months.

settings.question: Does it work on the visible veins I already have?
settings.answer: No. Vessels already structurally built don't get reversed by a serum — that's a laser conversation. This acts on the reactivity: how easily it starts, how high it goes, how long it takes to leave.

settings.question: What happens at week eight if it worked?
settings.answer: Most people move to once daily and stay there. It isn't a course you finish — the loop has no permanent off switch, and we'd rather say that now than at the point you'd feel misled. What changes is where it sits when you stop paying attention to it.
